label: January–June 1882
atlas_dek: The episodes reported from January through June 1882 in our dossiers that involve anti-Black violence or threats, placed on 1910 county lines and by month (some events were first reported the month after). Lynchings of white, Mexican and Native American victims, and lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are in the dossiers but not on the map. Hover for a short summary; select a dot to read the account in the sidebar. Drafts: no entry has had human review.
reader_intro:
Dossiers for 181 episodes reported from January through June 1882. Like 1881, this collection covers two things: lynchings and attempted or threatened lynchings of any race, and anti-Black violence or threats more broadly. Lynchings of white, Mexican and Native American victims, and lynchings where no report gives the victim’s race, are in the dossiers; only the anti-Black episodes are on the map. The episodes come from the located events in each month’s table, which include events from the month before that were first reported later, and from searches for victims in the Beck–Tolnay and Monroe Work Today inventories that the month runs missed. The search used white papers only. Events from December 1881 first reported in these months were moved to the 1881 collection.

We wrote 217 dossiers; 36 are set aside, and 68 more events got no dossier because the table alone showed them out of scope or already in 1881. Set aside: four legal executions reported as violence (at Mansfield, Austin, Lakeport and Greenville, South Carolina); 5 duplicates; reports that proved false, hypothetical or about an earlier year; and events with no force, no Black target, or no racial element outside a lynching.

Inventory differences are kept and noted, not counted. Beck–Tolnay lists James M. Davis, a revenue officer ambushed by moonshiners near McMinnville, Tennessee, in March, as lynched; our papers describe an ambush of an officer, which our rules do not count as a lynching. Calvin Luckey’s lynching in Randolph County, West Virginia, is counted as probable: local papers denied it.

Police violence is kept generously: men shot while fleeing or resisting arrest are included, and only gunfights over an arrest or a crime in progress are set aside from the totals. Two-sided fights and threats with no force stay in the reader but out of the totals.

Method: a research agent (Sonnet) searched the papers. A write-up agent (Opus) wrote the dossier with keyed citations, and a code check confirmed every quote and citation against the article text. A coding agent (Sonnet) then read each dossier and recorded who acted, what they did and to whom, and what the reports suggest lay behind a killing; the type, the lynching stage and whether an episode counts are derived from those codes by fixed rules. Where the rules flag a hard case, a second coding agent reads the dossier independently, and cases where the two readings disagree are marked “Disputed coding.” White-press clippings are page images where we could place them on the scan, otherwise text.

Drafts: entries have not had human review, except the scope rulings noted in the codebook.
